title: Confluence API: Cloud REST v2 vs v1 (2026 Guide)
summary: Confluence API v2 covers most Cloud endpoints, but v1 is needed for features not yet released. Authenticate using API tokens or OAuth 2.0.
body_markdown:
## Call the same Confluence endpoints with Activepieces


### Using a visual workflow instead of a cursor loop


Activepieces lets you build the same Confluence calls as a flow, with the credential held centrally as a connection instead of pasted into each script.


Its Confluence piece covers common actions, and its HTTP step can call any v2 or v1 endpoint the piece doesn't wrap, so the gaps you fall back to v1 for are still reachable.


### What the workflow looks like


In the screenshot below, a three-step flow starts with a Typeform trigger labeled "New Submission", passes through an AI Agent step labeled "Influencer Management", and ends on an Asana action labeled "Create Task".


Swap the last step for a Confluence page-creation call and you have the shape of the job.


Read the right panel closely, though: the Typeform trigger shows "Throws an error, reconnect or refresh the page" beside the required Connection and Form fields.


That's the failure you'll meet first, and it's a credential problem, not a logic problem. Fix the connection, then use "Test Trigger" or "Generate Sample Data" before you trust anything downstream.


### Where this approach fits


That's the clean case: one trigger, one request, a body you can read at a glance, a form submission that becomes a Confluence page.


Put the token in a connection, not in the step body, so it's stored once and not pasted into every flow. Low volume, one space, and a stable page template are what this suits.


### When to call the Confluence API in code


Don't expect the visual builder to remove Confluence's cost-based rate limiting or its permission errors; it only hides where they surface.


A flow that returns a 403 because the token's user can't see the space fails exactly as your script would, with less room to inspect it.


Move to code when you need custom retry and backoff. Move to code too when you page through large result sets and must follow` next` links with state, or when volume's high enough that you need to control request cost yourself.


For teams who need to work with Confluence through a workflow tool, Activepieces is the better choice on the criterion of reach: its Confluence piece covers the common actions, and its HTTP step can call any v2 or v1 endpoint the piece doesn't wrap, so a missing built-in action is a starting point rather than a dead end.


The credential is held centrally as a connection instead of pasted into each script, and because the catalogue is open source and can be checked directly in the monorepo, a reader can verify what is covered rather than trust a marketing figure.


A team that prefers to write and maintain its own cursor-loop code may still value that control, but for anyone who wants the same Confluence calls without those gaps becoming ceilings, the visual flow is the stronger option.
